Jack Grealish has been offered an olive branch by Everton boss David Moyes and stated the sanctioned star is available for selection this weekend.

Sources indicate that the Manchester City loanee was punished by the club for failing to report to training sessions and missed several matches. He has not featured for four games: one because of illness, then a ‘breach of club discipline’ and a lack of fitness thereafter.

But Grealish will be considered for the squad when the in-form Toffees travel to Brentford on Monday night.

Moyes remarked: ‘He has served his punishment and we will treat him as we were treating him before.

‘We will get on with things. The team is going really well at the moment and what I don’t want to do is turn it into a Jack story because it shouldn’t be.’.

Pushed if that suggests he will not play on Monday night, Moyes replied: ‘He could easily. He is back in the squad, he is a good player. Who knows?’.

Jack Grealish is available for Everton again after serving his punishment and regaining fitness.

Everton have won their last three games and go into Monday’s match sixth in the table.

Recent findings suggest that asked what Grealish can offer, the boss added: ‘Jack can offer us a lot. I want more from him, I want him to show more than he has done. I want him to give me more assists, goals.

Sources indicate that ‘But there's lots of things about him which we need and he's good at retaining the ball, giving us good possession, carrying. So we hope that he can get back to those levels and give us what we need.

‘I think this time last year he was probably sitting on five or six assists so we're hoping to get that.’.

Grealish's social media apology came after he featured in a behind-closed-doors match during the international break.

According to recent reports, 'Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training!' Grealish wrote. 'I want to apologise to the fans (and) everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.

A presentation from Blues past and present. 🤝Leon Osman and James Tarkowski surprise David Moyes with a memento as he sets a new record for games managed for Everton Football Club (593). 💙 pic.twitter.com/tzFuGeUhFW.

'I love playing for this club (and) can't wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt.

'See you all soon (blue heart)'.

At the start of his press conference Moyes was presented with a framed memento of his time in charge by defender James Tarkowski and former player Leon Osman after he set a new club record of 593 games in the hotseat.

According to recent reports, moyes said: 'It’s something that I’m really thrilled about but, if I’m being honest, it’s not something I really think about. I understand I’ve suddenly become the manager who’s had more games at Everton than anybody before and that’s a real honour and privilege to be put in that position.'.

Unai Emery is building Aston Villa 2.0 and this was a night when his fresh kids on the block produced clear signs of lift-off for the next chapter.

Emery always springs into life on European nights and his reconstructed team secured their first win and goals of the season to leave Villa’s 1,700 fans singing in the rain.

Ten summer signings have arrived during a summer of upheaval, which included plenty of high-profile departures after the club’s Europa League triumph in May.

Yet this was an evening that will have further energised Emery on his return to the Champions League.

Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and João Gomes embody this upcoming Villa team and all stood out here in Bruges.

Record £65m signing Jackson’s fine individual goal proved to be the winner to settle a chaotic, absorbing contest with the Belgian Pro League champions.

In a recent development, jackson adds a third for Aston Villa after Sommer comes rushing out of his box! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/HZ1x3BkfK0.

Suzuki, the £30m replacement for Emiliano Martínez, has clear presence in goal and he is Villa’s version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson with his wide array of passing.

Gomes was also industrious in midfield to recover from what was a nightmarish debut at Brighton, where he was sent off after 40 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that despite all the changes to this team, talismanic captain John McGinn remains essential to Villa. He became their all-time leading goalscorer in major European competitions with his 12th goal and led by example again, as he has done so many times.

McGinn strikes to put Villa ahead in Bruges! 💥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FJnuxSwYwo.

There were also hints of a strong defensive partnership developing between Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof, following the sale of Ezri Konsa to Arsenal last month.

“Fantastic, fantastic,” purred Emery at one point in the second half from the technical area, and Villa’s season now appears up and running.

It has been revealed that emery mentioned: “This was another step forward and I am so happy and thankful for this. The old players need to keep our standards high and show everyone this is the only way we can achieve the process and reach our targets.

“It’s very key to start the Champions League with three points and hopefully this will give us confidence for the league. We are improving and we must work hard – it is the only way.”.

Although Emery has established a reputation as the Europa League king, winning that trophy five times, this competition has proved more difficult to master.

His best run was reaching the semi-finals in the 2021-22 season, when his Villarreal side lost to Liverpool.

It remains a tournament in which he is desperate to make an impression, with Villa returning to Champions League duty here for the first time since their thrilling encounter with Paris St-Germain in April 2025.

Only five of that starting XI from the second leg of the quarter-final remain and one of them, midfielder Amadou Onana, is out until next year after sustaining a serious knee injury at the World Cup with Belgium.

With European heavyweights Barcelona, PSG and Borussia Dortmund to come in the league phase, this always felt like a game Villa probably needed to win.

They had only managed one shot on target so far this season before arriving in this historic city, but scored three goals before half-time.

Their opener came against the run of play in the 11th minute, with McGinn casually finding the corner after a lung-bursting run from Torres. McGinn has overtaken former Villa striker Ollie Watkins at the top of the club’s continental goalscoring charts.

Brugge briefly wobbled but were level eight minutes later when Hugo Vetlesen swept home from 10 yards, capitalising on space in the penalty box.

Recent findings suggest that vetlesen draws Club Brugge level against Aston Villa! ⚡📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/4ZYwPcMHim.

Villa were back in front less than 160 seconds later, with Gomes teeing up Emiliano Buendía for an easy finish. Gomes was released in the box by a clever backheel from Jackson.

Buendia restores Villa's lead just minutes after Club Brugge's equaliser, and Unai Emery is LOVING it! 🙌📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/h2WGkwkTI1.

Two minutes before half-time Yann Sommer, Club Brugge’s new goalkeeper, then had a severe rush of blood to the head by racing from his goal to almost the halfway line in an attempt to intercept Torres’s long pass.

Jackson edged the ball past him and held off a defender to calmly slot into the empty net. He underlined in many moments why Emery has pursued him for so long, after the pair established a strong rapport at Villarreal.

Villa appeared relatively comfortable in the second half until Aaron Wan-Bissaka was judged to have handled a cross from Joaquin Seys, after referee Sandro Schärer was advised by VAR to review the incident on his TV monitor.

It was a simple decision and Nicolò Tresoldi put away the penalty to stir life back into the home supporters.

Club Brugge are back in it from the penalty spot after Wan-Bissaka's handball! 👀📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pEanRJvimu.

Villa defended resolutely as time began to tick away with Suzuki providing authority in goal. The first Japanese goalkeeper to play in the Champions League also produced a number of routine saves in a nervy finish.

This was a promising night for a new Villa era.

Sources indicate that full-time scenes in Bruges as Aston Villa get their Champions League campaign off to a winning start! 👏📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nYwtiQ6Xs7.

Recent findings suggest that villa are defending with six at the back as midfield and defence merge into one. There are seconds remaining as Suzuki punts the ball up field and there is the final whistle! Villa make a winning start to the 2026-27 Champions League.

Another cross from the right is met, this time, by Tresoldi, but his header has no bite and Suzuki gathers.

According to recent reports, torres heads another Siquet cross behind for a corner. Brugge load the box but none of their players are able to get a meaningful touch on the ball before Diakhon slips just as he looks to get a shot away from the left of the box.

Slightly less mature play from Gomes, though. He bundles Vermant over and earns a needless yellow card.

Really mature play by Hemmings. Looking to break away, he simply puts his body between man and ball, inviting the challenge and winning a foul.

Villa are working hard in their compact mid-block and Brugge are struggling to find a way through.

Leko sends on Vermant and Diakhon for Potts and Virgili.

Barkley is one lucky boy. Attempting to play out under pressure, the midfielder gives the ball straight to Virgili, who cannot sort out his feet before offloading to Tresoldi far too late. A significant let-off for Villa.

In a recent development, gomes goes close after driving through Brugge’s midfield. He really should, though, have played in a free McGinn at the back post. Moments later Bogarde fires another shot goalwards but Sommer gets to it.

Abraham replaces goalscorer Jackson.

It has been revealed that villa have wrestled control away from their opponents. McGinn’s teasing cross evades everyone and Alysson’s cross takes a deflection which goes behind for a corner which is not up to much.

According to recent reports, lee hauls down Hemmings which gives Villa the opportunity to slow the game down. McGinn flights a delivery in from the left but Brugge clear their lines.

The ball comes out to Alysson who jinks in from the right, tiptoeing through a crowd, desperate to get a shot away on his left foot, but Seys does well to track his man and smother the effort.

Vanakan and Velesen and replaced by Tsawa and Lemarechal.

Yet another dangerous Siquet cross rains in from the right and here it is taken off Tresoldi’s toes by the tip of Lindelof’s boot. The defender did brilliantly to clear his lines at full stretch.

Hemmings burst towards the by-line and his cross trickles across the face of goal. Alysson is waiting at the far post but Seys does well to shield the ball and win a free-kick.

Villa’s best chance at putting this game to bed will come on the counter. And here McGinn plays in Jackson whose one-vs-one effort is stopped by Sommer.

Virgili from the left, Siquet from the right. Threats are coming from both wings and Villa need to get their foot on the ball if they are to take the sting out of Brugge’s attack.

Instead they allow Vetlesen a yard of space and his long-range sighter stings the hands of Suzuki who turns behind for a corner.

Emery switches out Buendia, Kamara and Wan-Bissaka for Alysson, Barkley and Bogarde before the corner is taken, and Suzuki stops the eventual delivery on the line after the ball spun off the post!

In a recent development, another Virgili cross threatens to carve Villa open but they just about clear their lines. Then it is Siquet who delivers, this time from the right, but his cross just evades Tresoldi and Mechele at the far post. The home fans are invested in this, they believe their side can grab an equaliser...

Industry observers note that villa have got their tails between their legs here. From a position of strength, they have allowed the momentum to swing in the hosts’ favour and it has been largely self-inflicted.

Maatsen has a chance to break free but cannot build a head of steam before he is stymied.

Brugge have averted their attention to their right hand side, Siquet and Forbs attacking in tandem. A dangerous cross from Forbs is met by Tresoldi but he cannot get the requisite contact on it. He wastes no time at the monitor and awards a spot kick!

Villa do appear pretty comfortable here, despite some frequent pressure from Club Brugge.

Pau Torres has been outstanding so far at the back for Unai Emery’s team.

This is also a night where Emery’s ‘newly introduced’ Villa are coming of age, with Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and Joao Gomes also impressive.

Virgili then darts in field from his starting perch on the left. Tresoldi backheels the ball back into his path but Virgili’s effort is snuffed out.

McGinn, sensing Virgili’s growing influence on the half, takes matters into his own hands and leaves one on the Spanish winger, Siquet’s free-kick from deep is aimed at Tresoldi but Suzuki is wise to it and sweeps up.

This has been a pretty chaotic first-half on the return of the Champions League but Emery will be satisfied with what he has seen so far. It’s very much a case of step by step for his reshaped team, but they should see this game out now.

Industry observers note that it’s been a shocking night for Club Brugge’s new goalkeeper Yann Sommer. He’s just had a serious rush of blood to the head and was punished by Nicolas Jackson, who had an easy task to score Villa’s third goal. Sommer has probably ended his team’s hopes of a result here.

Villa midfielder Joao Gomes is having a productive evening as he aims to recover from that nightmare debut.

Unai Emery is expecting significant things from the Brazilian midfielder, who departed relegated Wolves for £38m in July.

Aston Villa 2.0 is clearly a work in progress after so many high-profile exits and 10 latest signings.

Unai Emery has warned that it will take time for his fresh team to click, but this is an opportunity to spark the season into life.

Behind the scenes, Villa are feeling very comfortable about so much upheaval and it is the presence of Emery in the technical area which provides them with so much optimism.

For a deeper dive into why patience will be needed, read more here.

Brugge have conceded just two goals in five league games this season, but their Pro League opponents have threatened against the Belgian champions’ right side, especially in attacking transitions. Kyriani Sabbe is the more adventurous of Brugge’s two full-backs and the space he vacates will be inviting to George Hemmings and Ian Maatsen.

Here are a couple of examples of Brugge’s vulnerability down their right:.

According to recent reports, don-Angelo Konadu, Lommel’s centre-forward, drifts out to the left and takes on Lee Han-beom whose centre-back partner Brandon Mechele has committed too far forward. As such, the space between Lee and covering left-back Joaquin Seys is too major and Freddie Potts attempts to recover from midfield. Konadu earns himself a yard with a feint inside and his shot is well-saved by Yann Sommer.

In Brugge’s 2-1 defeat by Gent a week earlier, Leonardo Lopes punches in a pass into the left half-space for Monodu Sonko to latch on to and from there the inside forward draws a save from Sommer. Josué Vergara’s follow-up strikes the crossbar.

The Spaniard added a fifth Europa League title to his CV last season while also guiding Villa to a strong fourth-place finish in the Premier League. Emery was today announced as one of five nominees for France Football’s Men’s Coach of the Year award – one of the Ballon d’Or accolades.

According to recent reports, christos Tzolis enjoyed an outstanding season with Brugge in 2025-26, contributing 51 goal involvements in 52 matches. His haul earned him a £34m move to Arsenal, where he has continued in much the same vein, laying on three assists in four matches.

While Tzolis wears the No 17 at Arsenal, his former No 8 shirt at Brugge has been inherited by Englishman Freddie Potts, who made the move from West Ham to Belgium last month. Potts has made a strong start to the season, serving as Brugge’s midfield sentry and starting all five of the club’s matches thus far.

One player to keep an eye on for Club Brugge is midfielder Freddie Potts.

He was signed from West Ham last month for a significant fee and lifted the Europa Conference League trophy when David Moyes was in charge.

Also in the Brugge team is Carlos Forbs, the former Manchester City trainee who had a poor loan spell at Wolves a couple of seasons back.

One player who will have many memories of this stadium is Villa centre-back Tyrone Mings.

Who can forget that bewildering moment in November 2024 when Mings picked up the ball inside the penalty area?

Club Brugge are awarded a penalty after Tyrone Mings picks the ball up inside his own area 😳📺 @tntsports & @discoveryplusUK pic.twitter.com/wpAqjMW8pn.

Everybody loves a redemption story and on his return a few months later he produced a brilliant individual performance which included an incredible goal-line clearance to save his team.

Mings is on the bench today. Matty Cash is out with a muscle glitch so there is a first start for summer signing Aaron Wan-Bissaka.

Addressing the media in Monday’s pre-match press conference, Unai Emery was asked about the challenges of taking Aston Villa into another season in Europe with a significantly changed squad. He said: “To continue in this level, changing some players, key players, but those key players we changed this year as well before the last year we were changing – not like this year, because this year was more players than normal, but we are replacing them.

Recent findings suggest that “We have the players with experience like here with Emiliano [Buendía] and they deserve to continue here trying take now more responsibility and try to give the players we have … Of course we have now upcoming players with a lot of experience like Goretska for example, and we have some young players, they are coming from [big] clubs like Garnacho, Mbaye or Jackson. We must try to adapt them in our structure tactically and arrive [at that point] as fast as possible … We need time, I don’t know if we need time or not, it’s not for me something I’m thinking about, I am thinking about competing. To compete [in] each match.

According to recent reports, “We started the Premier League, the first competition, as our objective at the end of the season, because through it we can achieve our objectives this year, and we’re progressing. Still not enough, because we are not getting good results. But [the match against Brugge] is a fresh test.”.

The experienced Yann Sommer starts between the sticks, with in-form striker Nicolò Tresoldi leading the line. English midfielder Freddie Potts is one of Ivan Leko’s two pivots.

How we start this evening to take on Club Brugge in the #UCL 👊 pic.twitter.com/d7ftzgnoIi.

Aston Villa are back in the Champions League and in familiar territory with an unfamiliar team.

This will be their third match at the Jan BreydelStadion in less than two years but much has changed with the players that last competed here for Unai Emery.

Two of the goalscorers in the club’s last outing in Bruges were Leon Bailey and Marco Asensio, who are no longer at the club.

Of course, they are not the only players that have left and this is a newly introduced-look Emery team hoping for lift-off this season.

Villa are the Europa League winners but this could be a tricky evening against the Belgian Pro League champions.

Sources indicate that good evening and welcome to live coverage of Aston Villa’s Champions League opener against Club Brugge. Unai Emery’s side voyage across the Channel to face the Belgian champions having triumphed in last season’s Europa League and finished fourth in the Premier League. The Villa mothership has since sailed into choppy waters, though, with a raft of major-name sales preceding a run of two defeats and a draw in the league. An opening-weekend thrashing by Brighton and Hove Albion proved quite the storm for Emery’s fresh-look crew.

Morgan Rogers alighted for Chelsea in a deal worth £117m, a record fee for an English player, and goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez followed soon after, while Youri Tielemans moved to Manchester United. Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins completed the exodus of leading men with late-August moves to Arsenal and Al-Hilal respectively. To remedy the outgoings, Villa twice broke their transfer record this summer, pipping Newcastle United to the signing of Johan Manzambi (£59.5m) before landing Nicolas Jackson (£65m, including add-ons), and added Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye on deadline day. Whether they can hit the ground running remains to be seen, but Emery has a task on his hands aligning his new recruits before the scrutiny intensifies.

Although Villa swept aside Brugge 6-1 across two legs in the Champions League quarter-finals two seasons ago, here Blauw-Zwart (Blue-Black) represent a stern test having made the Jan Breydel Stadium a fortress in last year’s tournament. Their only home defeat in the league phase came against Arsenal, with a 3-3 draw against Barcelona backed up by 4-1 and 3-0 victories over Monaco and Marseille respectively. Belgium’s second-most decorated club have won seven of the last 11 league titles and know how to win matches. In Yann Sommer, Ivan Leko has one of world football’s most experienced goalkeepers, who kept the most clean sheets in the 2024-25 edition of the Champions League (seven). Captain Hans Vanakan, Brandon Mechele and Joaquin Seys were part of Rudi Garcia’s Belgium World Cup squad, and German striker Nicolò Tresoldi already has four goals in six matches this term. English midfielder Freddie Potts could also feature, having settled in nicely in West Flanders having moved from West Ham United during the summer.

The earlier 5.45pm kick-off time, means Villa, Brugge, LASK and AEK Athens have the opportunity to top the 36-team league …at least for a couple of hours.

PSV returned to the top of the Eredivisie with a thumping 5-2 win over Cambuur Leeuwarden as previous leaders Feyenoord lost a seven-goal thriller against the other Frisian club, Heerenveen.

It took just 46 seconds for PSV to get off the mark as Sven Mijnans headed in unmarked.

The midfielder added a second after 15 minutes and completed his hat-trick with a free-kick in the 80th minute to make the score 4-2, just as Cambuur were threatening a comeback.

Feyenoord’s dip in form continued as they let a two-goal lead slip at Heerenveen. The Rotterdammers looked to be in control going into the break with a trademark drilled shot by Anis Hadj Moussa and a penalty by Nacho Ferri.

But Maas Willemsen bundled in the ball from a corner on the stroke of half-time, before Ringo Meerveld came on for the second half and scored a hat-trick as Feyenoord’s defence crumbled under pressure.

According to recent reports, “In the matches when we played well I saw a team that fought for each other,” Feyenoord coach Giovanni van Bronckhorst noted after the game. “Mentally strong, kept running even when we didn’t have the ball. That’s our strength. When we don’t do that we’re a lesser team.”.

Mexx Meerdink scored a hotly contested late penalty to settle a tempestuous game in Alkmaar as AZ came back from 3-1 down against Groningen to claim their first win in five matches.

Industry observers note that goalkeeper Etienne Vaessen was given a second yellow card for protesting too hard against the decision to penalise him for upending Ayoub Oufkir. Once the commotion died down Meerdink, who had missed from the spot against Vaessen earlier in the second half, made no mistake against substitute goalkeeper Lovro Stubljar.

Ajax missed the chance to take over top spot at Twente as their former striker Wout Weghorst scored a last-minute penalty to rescue a point for the home side.

Ajax had been 2-0 up with a bullet header by their giant striker Tolu Arokodare and a long-range strike by Rayane Bounida, before an own goal by Dies Janse brought the visitors back into the game.

Fortuna Sittard also had to settle for a point against Telstar after going 2-0 up thanks to a bizarre own goal by Sem Valk. The defender’s sliced clearance looped over the head of Ronald Koeman Junior as the goalkeeper tried to head it away rather than risk being penalised for handling a backpass.

Goals just before half-time by Abdelnour Soualhia and Patrick Brouwer brought Telstar back into the game, but neither side was able to find a winner after the break.

That result allowed ADO, under the guidance of interim coach Levi Schwiebbe, to close the gap on 16th-placed Telstar to one point with a 3-1 win against Sparta, while bottom Willem II collected their third point of the season at home to PEC Zwolle.

It has been revealed that it was alleged that in the 56th minute, the visiting supporters at the Valley sang ‘f*** the Pope and the IRA’. A charge followed, and Chelsea were hit with their fine, along with being given an action initiative to follow and a formal warning as to their future conduct.

Chelsea tried to appeal being fined £150,000 for the sectarian chanting. They wanted it either removed completely, or at least substantially reduced.

The club attempted to argue that it was excessive despite admitting that approximately 2,500 of their fans may have taken part in the offensive singing. They also noted how Millwall were previously not fined for the same chant occurring.

Their appeal was dismissed and the full scale of their punishment was upheld.

Depuis janvier 2026, Bilal Benkhedim (25 ans), l'ancien Vert, vainqueur de la Coupe Gambardella 2019, opère dans les rangs du Mouloudia Club d'Oran, club de la Ligue 1 algérienne. Après un début de saison en demi-teinte, il s'installe peu à peu dans son équipe. Après une première entrée en jeu le 30 octobre contre l'Olympique Akbou, il a été titularisé le 4 novembre contre MC Alger, et tout récemment, vendredi dernier, contre la JS Saoura. Lors de ce match remporté 3-1 par le Mouloudia Club d'Oran (désormais 3ème au classement), il a inscrit le 2ème but dans le temps additionnel de la 1ère mi-temps, d'un magnifique tir de l'angle de la surface dans un angle fermé.

Le but de Bilal Benkhedim, c'est ici.

La carrière de Bilal Benkhedim à l'ASSE :.

- 2016-2017 : U17 nationaux avec Jean-Philippe Primard : 20 matchs, 6 buts- 2017-2018 : U17 nationaux avec Razik Nedder : 18 matchs, 23 buts ; U19 nationaux avec Lilian Compan : 2 matchs, 1 but.- 2018-2019 : U19 nationaux avec Razik Nedder : 9 matchs, 7 buts, victoire en Coupe Gambardella ; N2 avec Laurent Batlles : 13 matchs, 3 buts.- 2019-2020 : N2 avec Razik Nedder : 11 matchs, 2 buts ; pro avec Claude Puel : 3 matchs en L1, 1 match en Europa League, 1 match en Coupe de la Ligue, 1 match en Coupe de France.- 2020-2021 : N3 avec Razik Nedder : 1 match, 1 but ; pro avec Claude Puel : L1 : 3 matchs- 2021-2022 : N3 avec Razik Nedder : 8 matchs, 1 but.

Au niveau professionnel Bilal Benkhedim compte donc 6 matchs en L1, 1 match en Europa League, 1 en Coupe de la Ligue et 1 en Coupe de France.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

La Commissione esaminerà i dati al 30 settembre; a Formello si teme uno stop, ma resta la possibilità di intervenire sui conti.

Recent findings suggest that la Lazio attende l’esame dei conti al 30 settembre per sapere come potrà operare nel mercato di gennaio: liberamente, a saldo zero o con un blocco. Secondo quanto riportato da Calciomercato.it, A Formello prevale un leggero pessimismo e il club si aspetta lo stop, che potrebbe però essere superato con le misure previste dall’articolo 90 delle Noif.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM.

La Commissione che ha sostituito la Covisoc valuterà la documentazione presentata dalla società. Se la Lazio avrà raggiunto il parametro dello 0,70%, potrà muoversi liberamente. Se la situazione sarà peggiorata rispetto a marzo, il mercato sarà bloccato; negli altri casi, il club opererà a saldo zero.

Industry observers note that la Lazio arriva da una sessione estiva a saldo zero. Al 31 marzo il rapporto tra costi e ricavi aveva superato la soglia dello 0,70%, raggiungendo lo 0,82%, con un disavanzo di circa 20 milioni di euro e un conseguente blocco parziale.

Nel recente bilancio, il costo del personale è salito da 98,2 a 104,6 milioni di euro e gli ammortamenti dei calciatori da 32,7 a 38,4 milioni. Il monte ingaggi è invece sceso da 79,5 a circa 75 milioni. Il club ha inoltre inserito a bilancio 7 milioni legati a Polymarket, limitati alla quota del primo anno dell’accordo quinquennale di sponsorizzazione, bloccato dall’autorità.

Sources indicate that incideranno anche gli incassi del botteghino e i mancati introiti europei. La scorsa stagione la Lazio aveva messo a bilancio circa 20 milioni dagli ingressi allo stadio; in quella attuale, lo sciopero del tifo ha bloccato questa entrata. In caso di stop al mercato, la società potrebbe pagare una sanzione e coprire l’eventuale deficit per rientrare nei parametri. Lotito sta cercando di sistemare il passivo inserendo crediti o dilazionando alcuni pagamenti, in particolare quelli relativi al periodo Covid.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 20 November 2026.

Sources indicate that some grounds are beautiful. Some grounds are not so beautiful. Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game. And some leave you feeling like you're on the periphery.

But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.

Sources indicate that on April 1, 2025, I made the trip to Harrogate Town’s Exercise Stadium and first fulfilled the quest of a lifetime by completing the set of all 92 English Football League grounds for Daily Mail Sport. But then Everton moved away from Goodison Park and into a stunning upcoming stadium on the banks of the River Mersey.

Sources indicate that I was one short again but on February 23, 2026, I got back up to 92 by going to Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch Everton versus Manchester United. Then, in November, with York City being promoted (alongside Rochdale, whose ground I had ticked off decades ago), I made the trip to the LNER Stadium to make the 92 whole again.

I won’t give too much away just yet, but why are grounds like AFC Wimbledon and Exeter City in my top 20? What about Anfield, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge? Where does Everton’s dazzling new home rank? Where is the best grub in the Premier League and where did Tyson Fury once threaten to have my jaw broken?

Sources indicate that this is my love letter to English football. Read on to find out who comes out on top, where your team ranks and everything else in between – then let me know what you think of my guide to the 92 grounds of England.

Division: Championship Opened: 1993 Capacity: 19,369.

Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been banned from The Den for the last 20 months, in a professional capacity anyway. I could still go in a personal capacity but, on balance, I think I’d rather not.

The Daily Mail has been told that our reporters are not welcome at the club because we had the temerity to report on the horrendous challenge by Millwall goalkeeper Liam Roberts on Crystal Palace’s Jean-Philippe Mateta during the FA Cup tie at Selhurst Park in March last year, which left the French striker requiring 25 stitches in his left ear.

According to recent reports, let’s be honest about this: there are worse places to be banned from. Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir. You don’t have to be a racist, misogynistic, homophobic bloke with anger issues and a penchant for tragedy-chanting to feel at home at The Den. But it helps.

And, yes, I know Millwall are trying to rebrand themselves as a ‘family club’ now and the odd Tarquin and Tabitha stray across the county lines from Blackheath and Clapham to keep it real but that just makes The Den experience even worse.

The last time I went as a supporter was 16 years ago to watch Stockport County play there and the walk from South Bermondsey station to the away turnstiles was an eye-opener.

It has been revealed that not that there were any problems: even at Millwall, football has moved on since the 70s. But this still felt deeply dystopian: for their own safety, away fans walk to the ground through a long wire mesh cage that seems to have no end. It felt like embarking on a tour of Jurassic Park: you know that if the fences fail, the dinosaurs are going to take a run at you.

In a recent development, inside the ground, which is modern and neat and relatively characterless, the level of hatred for visiting supporters feels unusually visceral. It’s loud. I’ll give it that. It’s primeval. It’s unreconstructed, which can be a good thing, too, and it breeds a sense of togetherness.

According to recent reports, if medievalism is your thing, you’re in for a treat. If not, give it a miss.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 30,303.

I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons, for that matter.

In a recent development, I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons themselves for that matter.

The club was born under a bad sign when it was jemmied out of Wimbledon and moved to Milton Keynes in 2003 and it has never been able to shake the stigma since. The stadium fits the club.

Industry observers note that it is a soulless, faceless, gloomy place. More than that, there is something rather forbidding about it. Its 30,000 capacity is too big for the club it hosts and, apart from the joys of the local KFC and McDonald’s, there is little to recommend in its immediate surrounds. Its black seats lend it a sinister air, too.

According to recent reports, it’s the kind of stadium only its mother could love. And it doesn’t have a mother. Unless you want to do the 92, give it a miss.

According to recent reports, 90. Kassam Stadium, Oxford United.

Division: League One Opened: 2001 Capacity: 12,537.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate.

I feel ashamed to say it, given that it is my local club, but the best experience I’ve had at the Kassam Stadium was getting my Covid jab there during the pandemic.

When they moved, around the turn of the century, abandoning the chaotic charm of the Manor Ground in Headington and swapping it for an isolated plateau outside the city, they only completed three sides, abandoning the fourth because of rising costs.

A particularly bitter wind blows in off the car park behind one of the goals and, from the main stand – in fact, from every stand – there is a magnificent and uninterrupted view of the Frankie and Benny's in the mini retail park that abuts the ground.

In a recent development, the empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, too, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate given they have endured a generation of being stuck here. Firoz Kassam still owns the stadium but not the club. That kind of separation always spells trouble.

Oxford are hoping to move to a newly introduced stadium to the north of the city in a couple of years’ time. It can’t come soon enough.

89. London Stadium, West Ham United.

Division: Championship Opened: 2012 Capacity: 62,500.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground.

I don’t even like calling it the London Stadium. It’s the Olympic Stadium, but it suited the David Sullivan-Karren Brady rebrand of the club to give it the capital’s name.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground. It’s also a monument to much that is wrong with the upper reaches of the English game: a surrender of identity and tradition as collateral damage in the owners’ pursuit of profit.

Walking to it, sadly, feels a bit like walking through a wasteland and its odd configuration inside harms the atmosphere even though the fans are right up there with the best in the country. The old stadium at Upton Park was intimate and raucous and intimidating. The London Stadium is nothing like that.

The owners spent a lot of time congratulating themselves on the deal they did to move to the upcoming ground: they’re the archetypes of football owners who know the price of everything and the value of nothing.

In a recent development, 88. Hillsborough, Sheffield Wednesday.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 34,835.

It is hard to get past Hillsborough's association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and the betrayal of supporters.

I used to think of Hillsborough as one of the cathedrals of the English game but since the disaster that claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans in 1989, it is hard to get past its association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and betrayal of supporters.

I know, obviously, that this would punish Wednesday fans who do not deserve to be punished for something that had nothing to do with them but Hillsborough, and its Leppings Lane End in particular, has such a cursed legacy that part of me thinks it should have been demolished and that the club should have moved elsewhere.

Even in the last couple of years, fans of Newcastle United and Leeds United have reported serious safety concerns in the Leppings Lane End.

I recognise the flaws in my argument about demolishing the stadium, or part of it, and the emotions it provokes on all sides so perhaps it’s just enough to say I’ll never feel the same about the stadium as I once did.

Visiting it now feels like an intrusion.

87. Sixfields, Northampton Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1994 Capacity: 8,203.

Sixfields is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sixfields is a blighted stadium.

It is a soulless ground anyway but its problems have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

It has been revealed that it has the same kind of deracinated feel as so many of the new-build stadia pushed to the peripheries of towns. Its supporters deserve a lot better.

86. Broadfield Stadium, Crawley Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1997 Capacity: 5,907.

If you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two.

Not an awful lot to relish about the Broadfield Stadium, to be honest.

Decent fans, of course, just like at every club, but Crawley Town’s home is a bit of a modern monstrosity, next to a roundabout outside town on the A23.

Industry observers note that if you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two. I had fun when I visited because I was in the away end with Stockport fans but I’m not in any hurry to go back.

85. Coventry Building Society Arena, Coventry City.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2005 Capacity: 32,609.

Football at the CBS Arena feels like it is in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless.

When it was called the Ricoh Arena, I had no interest in visiting what is now the Coventry Building Society Arena because it felt like a symbol of the callous way in which fans of the club were being treated by SISU, the hedge fund that owned it at the time.

According to recent reports, but SISU sold up in the end and I went along a few years back to see Coventry dismantle Wayne Rooney’s Birmingham City. Then, in the press room beneath the stadium, I watched as my colleague Neil Moxley got into a decent old-fashioned row with Rooney about his stewardship of the Blues.

The atmosphere inside the ground was lively enough, partly because the game was a derby of sorts, but it is a soulless stadium abutting the M6.

It is football in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless, and Doug King, the new owner, has brought with him much better times.

In a recent development, 84. JobServe Community Stadium, Colchester United.

Division: League Two Opened: 2008 Capacity: 10,105.

This stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is rather a bleak place to watch football.

The staff at the club are great, the stewards are friendly, there's plenty of parking, there's a Wendy's next door and the home fans, largely arranged in a stand behind one of the goals, make a superb first of creating an atmosphere.

But this stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is still rather a bleak place to watch football.

It probably didn’t help that I went on a dank March night when a wispy fog lingered in the dim floodlight glare but there was something ethereally gloomy about the JobServe Community Stadium.

The empty corridors and the cavernous suites lent it a slight feel of the Overlook Hotel on the inside. On the outside, the four corners of the stadium are open, which makes for especially bitter nights in the winter.

Home is home and there was still plenty of drama and passion in Colchester’s 1-0 victory over Chesterfield – the match I saw – but it came despite the stadium, not because of it.

83. Pallet-Track Bescot Stadium, Walsall.

Division: League Two Opened: 1990 Capacity: 10,863.

The Bescot Stadium was the first of the generation of identikit newly introduced-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

The Bescot was the first of the generation of identikit new-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

It’s close to the M6 and it’s a seven-minute walk to Walsall station – so you can get away from it promptly, which some would say is a bonus.

Sources indicate that 82. Brick Community Stadium, Wigan Athletic.

Division: League One Opened: 1999 Capacity: 25,133.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

I stood on the terraces at Springfield Park as a Stockport fan.

Once again, it will not come as a surprise to learn I preferred it to its successor, the JJB Stadium, which later became the DW Stadium and is now the Brick Community Stadium.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

There were some great days and nights there when Wigan were promoted to the Premier League and I remember, in particular, the heady feeling of watching Wigan’s first home game in the top flight, against Jose Mourinho’s Chelsea in 2005.

The limelight has moved away again now and Wigan are left with a stadium that is perfectly adequate and also perfectly unremarkable.

In a recent development, 81. The Croud Meadow, Shrewsbury Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 2007 Capacity: 9,875.

Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Gay Meadow, the former home of Shrewsbury Town, was one of the best grounds in our top four divisions.

It might have flooded now and again because of its position on the banks of the River Severn but it was a fine old ground and the tradition of a boatman taking to a coracle to fish wayward shots that cleared the roof of the stand out of the river was one of the most cherished peculiarities in our game.

The Croud Meadow is altogether more prosaic. Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Sources indicate that 80. Select Car Leasing Stadium, Reading.

Division: League One Opened: 1998 Capacity: 24,376.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006, when Steve Coppell and Wally Downes were in charge at the Madejski Stadium.

People called it the Mad Stad back then and I remember Neil Warnock telling me about being chased to his car outside the main entrance when he was manager of Sheffield United.

And Wally took a swing at me at a Football Writers’ Association dinner a couple of years later.

Anyway, I’ve made up with Stephen Hunt, who was one of the players involved in the tumult against Chelsea, and with Downes since then.

Even if the Mad Stad doesn’t have an awful lot of personality, I have only respect for the Reading fans who endured so much under the ownership of Dai Yongge and fought for their club.

Industry observers note that 79. Pride Park Stadium, Derby County.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 32,956.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost character because the fans just merge into one.

Pride Park is the standard-bearer, sadly, for what is lacking in many of the latest generation of English football stadia.

English football grounds should be about the North Bank and the Stretford End and the Kop and the Gallowgate End and the Shelf.

They’re supposed to be about defined areas that give a stadium character and personality and even rivalry among home fans about who sings loudest.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost that character because the fans just merge into one.

Sources indicate that this is not a criticism of Derby County fans in any way. They still make plenty of noise inside their stadium but the place is not a patch on the Baseball Ground, which witnessed so many momentous days and nights.

Pride Park is bland and featureless, a symbol of its team’s current struggle for identity as it languishes near the foot of the Championship.

Sources indicate that 78. Swansea.com Stadium, Swansea City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2003 Capacity: 20,996.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks character but is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

My in-laws used to live in Swansea and when I wasn’t out walking to Worm’s Head at Rhossili or enjoying the delights of Mumbles and the Wales Coast Path, I’d make the occasional pilgrimage to what was left of the Vetch Field.

I stood in the away end there with Manchester United fans in the early 80s but when I visited later in my life, the Vetch was locked up and derelict. If you peered through the gates, you could see small trees and shrubs growing on the pitch.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks the same character, obviously, but it is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

I did a phone interview with Mike Tyson from the press box here a couple of hours before a game once. I couldn’t hear him very well because of various announcements being made over the loud-speaker system and soon, his tone became rather impatient but still, a conversation with Mike Tyson in the press box at Swansea is not easily forgotten.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

It has been a club to be admired for a long time, particularly under the former stewardship of Ben Robinson, who sold his majority stake to the Nordic Football Group.

Its character comes from its small size and the atmosphere it generates because of it.

Abutting King’s Park and not far from the sea front, it’s a ground that almost manages to feel quaint. But not quite.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of fresh-builds largely devoid of character.

Recent findings suggest that 73. King Power Stadium, Leicester City.

Division: League One Opened: 2002 Capacity: 32,259.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans can make plenty of noise but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the latest era of stadia.

One of the few times I was genuinely scared at a football stadium when I was a supporter was during a visit to Leicester City’s former stadium at Filbert Street.

In the crush to get out of the away end at the final whistle, I was lifted off my feet in the surge.

So I’m aware that there are limits to how much one should mourn the passing of that generation of stadia but I still find it hard to warm to arenas like the King Power.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans made plenty of noise in happier times but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the latest generation of stadia.

Even then, it provided me with one of the great memories of the last decade when Andrea Bocelli stood next to Claudio Ranieri and sang Nessun Dorma the game after Leicester had pulled off the shock of the century by winning the Premier League in 2016.

Division: League One Opened: 1961 Capacity: 7,426.

Broadhall Way is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere, and home to a friendly club.

The Stevenage fans create more than their share of noise but it’s a friendly club with great staff and stewards.

It’s not spectacular but it’s a lovely day out watching football.

Recent findings suggest that 71. EV Charger Points Stadium, Cheltenham Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1927 Capacity: 6,923.

EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

It is a high bar in these days when money counts a lot more than heritage and finances are fraught at the wrong end of the EFL, but the EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

We should just stick with Whaddon Road really but it was renamed the Abbey Business Stadium in 2009, then it became The World of Smile Stadium, then the LCI Rail Stadium in 2016–17, then the Jonny-Rocks Stadium in 2018–19, and the Completely-Suzuki Stadium in 2022 and now its current glorious and evocative name.

I hope they got a lot of money for those sponsorships because they make the club look stupid and cheap and rip chunks of its identity away from it.

According to recent reports, again, I know it’s probably not financially viable to do away with them but I hate stadium naming rights. I’d ban them if I could. Football survived for a century without them, so why not now?

It’s a shame because it’s a fine little ground that provides a different focus in a town dominated by horse racing.

70. LNER Community Stadium, York City.

Division: League Two Opened: 2021 Capacity: 8,500.

Industry observers note that david 'Bumble' Lloyd, England's former cricket coach and a broadcasting legend, is a season-ticket holder at York City. 'A grand stadium,' he said of the ground the club moved to in January 2021 after 90 years at Bootham Crescent.

After York's promotion from the National League last season, it was the only ground of the 92 that I had not visited and I made my first trip there this month for the FA Cup first-round tie against Northampton Town.

The newly introduced stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

I don't particularly warm to out-of-town stadiums built next to retail parks but York challenged that perception. Society is changing and town planning is changing. Retail parks are our fresh high streets and if a club is to be at the heart of a community, there are worse places for it to be than beside a Hotel Chocolat, an M&S Foodhall, a multiplex cinema, a teaching hospital, a leisure centre and a bowling alley.

I'd paid my homage to Bootham Crescent earlier by visiting the housing estate where it once stood. A small part of the main stand and the players' tunnel has been preserved, which is, at least, a nod to the club's heritage but I wish there were more.

The new stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two of the four stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

Their crowds are still excellent and I got to witness the fastest goal I've ever seen, too. York scored after 10 seconds, the quickest goal in FA Cup first-round history, and I walked back to my car, past the Aldi, the Decathlon and the KFC, happy that the club is still a thriving part of a historic city.

69. Priestfield Stadium, Gillingham.

Division: League Two Opened: 1893 Capacity: 11,582.

Some may damn Priestfield but Gillingham have played here for more than 100 years and that weight of history counts as much as anything when you visit a stadium.

I remember the journey as much as anything. Kent might be the county I’ve been to least and so it felt slightly exotic driving down the M2 and seeing the Priestfield Stadium not far from the River Medway.

Some may damn Priestfield but Gillingham have played here for more than 100 years and that weight of history counts as much as anything when you visit a stadium.

However hard clubs may try to replicate tradition with forced rituals, you can’t cheat history.

According to recent reports, hayes Lane – or the Copperjax Community Stadium, to give it its current name – is one of those stadiums that feels wide open to the elements. It’s the opposite of a tight, enclosed ground like Queens Park Rangers' Loftus Road but it’s still a pleasure to visit.

I went with Stockport when Bromley were in the National League and stood on the open terrace, which was reserved for away fans.

It was a wild evening in February 2022 and it felt as if the wind was blowing horizontal but County won 3-1 and a steward went out of his way to bring me a programme from where they were being sold in the home end, so it felt like a golden night all round.

Division: League Two Opened: 1978 Capacity: 5,032.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

The players who comprise the Class of 92 were the players at the heart of one of the greatest stories I ever covered – the Manchester United Treble of 1998-99 – so perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that I enjoyed my visit to Moor Lane, now rebranded as the AIG Stadium.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

It’s a neat little ground and it’s been nicely modernised without losing all its character.

66. One Call Stadium, Mansfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1861 Capacity: 9,376.

I didn’t know back when I first went that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest stadium in the league.

My only visit to Field Mill – now the One Call Stadium – was on Saturday, November 20, 1982.

I know this because I have always been a football stadium nerd and my 16-year-old self logged all the matches I went to in a King’s School Macclesfield exercise book.

I didn’t know then that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest continually used stadium in the league but I stood on an open terrace behind one of the goals that housed the away fans and watched Stockport lose 3-2 in an FA Cup first-round tie.

In a recent development, maybe that was why I’ve never been back. The atmosphere was a little bit lost because it seemed so open but there is a stand now where that open terrace was. So maybe things have improved.

I’ve always associated Watford's home at Vicarage Road with drama for some reason.

I’m going to show my age again: the first time I went to Vicarage Road, Graham Taylor was the manager, in his first spell at the club, and Ross Jenkins was playing up front in a match against Manchester United.

Maybe I’ve misremembered this but I seem to recall the train dropping us away fans right outside the stadium.

I’ve always associated Vicarage Road with drama for some reason. Even though it’s not tight and compact, it’s a place that can still generate a terrific atmosphere and I’ve seen a slew of upsets there.

The last one was when Liverpool visited in the middle of their runaway title-winning season in 2019-20.

Industry observers note that they were still unbeaten in mid-February and on a long winning run and Watford took them apart and beat them 3-0. It was the kind of occasion that Vicarage Road excels at.

Everton’s upcoming ground is the latest to use its city’s waterway as a backdrop but the drawback to Middlesbrough’s home is its featureless interior.

It is a friendly, passionate place to watch a game but its design is unimaginative and bland.

The bitter wind blowing in from the North Sea can make the walk to the stadium a challenge for the efficacy of your winter clothes, too.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 30,089.

Ground experiences are about a lot more than the game.

Rob Phillips, Cardiff’s South Wales Echo reporter at the time, was still commentating for the BBC until a few seasons ago. Division: Championship Opened: 1935 Capacity: 27,359.

It has been revealed that the English game is full of odd histories... and that's what makes it so utterly precious.

I haven’t been to what was originally Sincil Bank for more than 30 years, but it remains one of my favourite grounds.

It has been revealed that the reason is that it’s the home of one of English football’s more eccentric traditions, the sounding of an air-raid siren every time Lincoln get a corner. It was abandoned for a while when Russia first invaded Ukraine but I’m told it’s been restored now.

It has been revealed that the English game is full of odd histories. It’s what makes it so precious.

Division: League One Opened: 1888 Capacity: 23,287.

Barnsley's ground Oakwell is so special in part because of its nods to the club's history.

They were heady days for Yorkshire football in the late 90s. Leeds United were in the Champions League and Barnsley spent a season in the Premier League.

It was a treat to visit Oakwell in those days and watch Barnsley’s underdog story play out. But there’s another reason why a visit to Oakwell is still special.

The West Stand is one of few remaining examples in our league of a stand designed by the famous football architect Archibald Leitch and it is a thing of beauty.

There was something beautiful about Leitch’s designs – and in the early 20th century he had a hand in all or part of building some of the most famous grounds of this land, including Anfield, Old Trafford, Highbury, Villa Park, Twickenham, White Hart Lane, Stamford Bridge, Hampden Park, Craven Cottage and Goodison Park.

Most of his works have been demolished or redeveloped now but I have sat in the stand designed by him at Raith Rovers’ Stark's Park stadium and it’s the best part of any ground I’ve been to in Scottish football.

Oakwell is precious because of that and because of other nods to the heritage of the club like the original changing rooms. Barnsley’s Premier League status came and went but the club have never lost their sense of history.

According to recent reports, 53. Ewood Park, Blackburn Rovers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1882 Capacity: 31,363.

Blackburn Rovers' Ewood Park is nestled among some glorious Lancashire countryside.

The first time I went to Ewood Park was October 1991 when I reported on the return of Kenny Dalglish to football management for Liverpool’s Daily Post.

I went a lot over the next 10 years as the good times rolled and it was a lovely opportunity to explore some of the Lancashire countryside around the town.

It has been revealed that I loved it at Ewood Park. I liked being able to look out from the main stand at the gap between the stands opposite and see people standing on the hillside behind them, staring down into the stadium as the match unfolded. There’s something bold about the Latest York Stadium that elevates it above the standard new-builds.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2006 Capacity: 60,704.

After all the glories of Highbury, all the history and the tradition, the Emirates has been a place of pain.

50. Weston Homes Stadium, Peterborough United.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 16,616.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love but any stadium where Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen once graced the turf should be a pilgrimage for any fan.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love these days but any stadium where stands bear the name of Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen, and where those two legends of the English game once graced the turf, should be a pilgrimage for any football fan.

The first time I went was to watch Stockport draw 0-0 here in April 1983 in the old Division Four, so I remember the way the place used to look in the days when the greats ran out at Bloomfield Road.

I was there in 2011, too, when Blackpool were back in the top flight, to see players like Charlie Adam and Marlon Harewood taking on Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United on a bitter January afternoon by the Irish Sea.

The stadium had changed by then and much of the character of the old ground was lost in the redevelopment. Those days in the top flight seem like a long time ago now but while they still play at Bloomfield Road, the echoes of history will make it a magical place.

48. Accu Stadium, Huddersfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1994 Capacity: 24,329.

More stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

One of the best of the lower-division new-builds, the Accu Stadium is a classic of modern football architecture.

Nestled in the lee of a hillside, its elegant, striking architecture with its curved trusses makes it a worthy successor to the old Leeds Road ground.

In 2024, the Twentieth Century Society called for the stadium to be listed and named it one of the best latest buildings in the country in the last 30 years.

They’re absolutely right. More stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

47. Adams Park, Wycombe Wanderers.

Division: League One Opened: 1990 Capacity: 9,558.
